list_projects.title: List the organization's projects
list_projects.description: Every project in the organization the PAT can see, with its id, name, visibility and state. Almost every other tool here is project-scoped, so this is normally the first call -- and the project NAME (not its id) is what the other tools' `project` argument takes, though either works.

state_filter.description: Only projects in this state. Defaults to wellFormed, the normal one.

items.description: id, name, description, url, state, visibility and lastUpdateTime.

get_project.title: Get a project
get_project.description: One project's id, description, visibility, capabilities and default team. The `id` here is what appears in webhook payloads and audit logs, so this is how you turn one back into a human-readable name.

include_capabilities.description: Include the version control and process template capabilities.

capabilities.description: versioncontrol and processTemplate, when asked for.

list_teams.title: List the teams in a project
list_teams.description: The teams defined in a project, each with its id, name and description. Teams own boards, iterations and area paths, so a team id is what most board-level queries need.

query_work_items.title: Find work items with a WIQL query
query_work_items.description:
Run a WIQL query and get back MATCHING IDS ONLY -- not the work items themselves. Fetch those with get_work_items, which takes up to 200 ids at a time. An agent that stops at this call will conclude the query returned nothing useful; it returned exactly what it is supposed to.
WIQL is SQL-shaped over work item fields: `SELECT [System.Id] FROM WorkItems WHERE [System.WorkItemType] = 'Bug' AND [System.State] = 'Active' ORDER BY [System.CreatedDate] DESC`. Field names are the internal reference names in square brackets, and `@Me`, `@Today` and `@Project` are the macros worth knowing.
Results are capped at 20,000 ids; a query above that fails rather than truncating, so add a date filter.
query_work_items.notes: Returns ids only. Pass them to get_work_items for the actual fields.

query.description: The WIQL query. Field names go in square brackets; @Me, @Today and @Project are available as macros.
query.example: SELECT [System.Id] FROM WorkItems WHERE [System.State] = 'Active' ORDER BY [System.ChangedDate] DESC

output.description: The matching work item ids, and the columns the query selected.

workItems.description: Each with id and url. Pass the ids to get_work_items.

get_work_items.title: Get several work items by id
get_work_items.description:
Fetch up to 200 work items in one call, with their fields. The natural follow-up to query_work_items.
`fields` limits what comes back to the reference names you name -- `System.Id,System.Title,System.State` -- which is much smaller than the default, since a work item carries a great many fields. Do not combine `fields` with `expand`; the API rejects that.
An id the PAT cannot see makes the whole call fail, so `error_policy` of `omit` is worth setting when the ids came from a broad query.
get_work_items.notes: Maximum 200 ids per call. fields and expand are mutually exclusive.

ids.description: Comma-separated work item ids, up to 200.

fields.description: Comma-separated field reference names to return, e.g. "System.Id,System.Title,System.State". Cannot be combined with expand.

expand.description: Extra data to include. Cannot be combined with fields.

error_policy.description: omit skips ids that cannot be read instead of failing the whole call. Worth setting when the ids came from a broad query.

as_of.description: Return the work items as they were at this ISO 8601 timestamp.

items.description: id, rev, fields (keyed by reference name) and url.

get_work_item.title: Get one work item
get_work_item.description:
A single work item with its fields, and optionally its relations -- the parent, children, related items and linked commits or pull requests that `expand: relations` returns.
That relation list is the only way to see what a work item is connected to; the fields alone do not carry it.

expand.description: relations includes parent, child and linked artifacts; all includes everything.

as_of.description: Return the work item as it was at this ISO 8601 timestamp.

rev.description: Its revision number; pass it to update_work_item to detect a concurrent edit.

fields.description: Field values keyed by reference name -- System.Title, System.State, System.AssignedTo and the rest.

relations.description: Parent, child, related and linked artifacts, when expanded.

create_work_item.title: Create a work item
create_work_item.description:
Create a bug, task, user story or any other type the project's process defines. The type goes in the URL with a `$` prefix, which this tool adds -- pass `Bug`, `Task` or `User Story` as `work_item_type`.
Under the hood this sends a JSON Patch document; the common fields are exposed as ordinary arguments, and `patch_operations` takes raw operations for anything else: `[{"op": "add", "path": "/fields/Microsoft.VSTS.Scheduling.StoryPoints", "value": 5}]`.
`assigned_to` wants the person's unique name -- their email address in most organizations -- not their display name. `area_path` and `iteration_path` are backslash-separated and start with the project name.
create_work_item.notes: Field names are internal reference names, not the labels the web UI shows.

work_item_type.description: The work item type as the process defines it -- Bug, Task, User Story, Feature, Epic. list_work_item_types gives the valid names.

title.description: The work item's title. The only field always required.

description.description: The description. HTML, not Markdown -- Azure DevOps renders this field as HTML. Bugs use Microsoft.VSTS.TCM.ReproSteps instead in some processes; use patch_operations for that.

assigned_to.description: Who to assign it to, by unique name -- normally their email address, not their display name.

state.description: Initial state. Valid values depend on the process -- New, Active, Resolved, Closed for Agile.

area_path.description: Area path, backslash-separated and starting with the project name.

iteration_path.description: Iteration path, backslash-separated and starting with the project name.

patch_operations.description: Extra JSON Patch operations for fields this tool does not expose, each {"op": "add", "path": "/fields/<ReferenceName>", "value": ...}.

validate_only.description: Run the process rules without creating anything. Useful for checking required fields.

rev.description: Its revision, 1 for a new item.

fields.description: The stored field values, including any the process filled in.

update_work_item.title: Update a work item
update_work_item.description:
Change fields on an existing work item. Like create_work_item this sends a JSON Patch document, with the common fields as arguments and `patch_operations` for anything else.
Only the fields you supply change; everything else is untouched, so this cannot accidentally clear a field the way a full-object PUT would.
Passing `rev` makes the update conditional on the work item still being at that revision, which is how you avoid overwriting someone else's edit -- get_work_item returns the current one.
update_work_item.notes: Only the fields supplied are changed. Pass rev to detect a concurrent edit.

assigned_to.description: Reassign to this person, by unique name (normally their email address).

state.description: A new state. The process may reject a transition that skips steps, or require other fields first -- a Resolved bug often needs a reason.

iteration_path.description: A new iteration path -- this is how an item is moved between sprints.

tags.description: Tags, semicolon-separated. REPLACES the existing tags rather than adding to them.

comment.description: A comment to add to the work item's discussion, written to System.History alongside the change.

rev.description: The revision you read. The update fails if the work item has changed since, instead of overwriting the other edit.

patch_operations.description: Extra JSON Patch operations for fields this tool does not expose.

validate_only.description: Run the process rules without saving anything.

output.description: The work item after the update.

delete_work_item.title: Delete a work item
delete_work_item.description:
Move a work item to the project's recycle bin, where it can be restored -- or, with `destroy` set, delete it permanently and irrecoverably.
Deleting a parent does not delete its children; they are left orphaned, which is usually not what anyone wants. Check `relations` with get_work_item first.
delete_work_item.notes: Goes to the recycle bin unless destroy is set, which is permanent. Child items are orphaned, not deleted.

destroy.description: Permanently destroy the work item instead of sending it to the recycle bin. There is no undo.

output.description: The deleted work item as it was.

list_work_item_types.title: List a project's work item types and their fields
list_work_item_types.description:
The work item types the project's process defines -- Bug, Task, User Story, or whatever a custom process calls them -- each with its fields and their reference names.
This is where the field reference names for create_work_item and update_work_item come from, and the only reliable way to know which states a type actually allows, since those vary by process template.

items.description: name, referenceName, description, fields (each with referenceName), states and transitions.

list_repositories.title: List a project's Git repositories
list_repositories.description: The Git repositories in a project, each with its id, name, default branch, size and clone URLs. The repository id or name is what every other Git tool here takes.

items.description: id, name, defaultBranch, size, remoteUrl, sshUrl and webUrl.

list_commits.title: List commits in a repository
list_commits.description:
Commits in a repository, newest first, with author, committer, message and change counts. Narrow with `search_branch` for one branch, `search_author` for one person, or the date arguments for a window.
`$top` defaults low on purpose -- an unbounded listing on a large repository is slow and rarely what is wanted.

search_branch.description: Only commits on this branch, by name without the refs/heads/ prefix.

search_author.description: Only commits by this author, by display name or email.

from_date.description: Only commits after this date, e.g. "2026-01-01".

skip.description: How many commits to skip, for paging.

items.description: commitId, author, committer, comment, changeCounts and remoteUrl.

list_pull_requests.title: List pull requests in a repository
list_pull_requests.description:
Pull requests in a repository, filtered by status, branch or author. `status` defaults to `active` in Azure DevOps, so an apparently empty result on a busy repository usually means everything is already completed -- pass `all` or `completed` to see those.
Branch arguments take the full ref: `refs/heads/main`, not `main`.
list_pull_requests.notes: Defaults to active pull requests only. Branch filters need the full refs/heads/ path.

status.description: Which pull requests to return. Defaults to active.

target_branch.description: Only pull requests into this branch, as a full ref.

source_branch.description: Only pull requests from this branch, as a full ref.

creator_id.description: Only pull requests created by this identity GUID.

reviewer_id.description: Only pull requests this identity GUID is a reviewer on.

top.description: How many pull requests to return.

skip.description: How many to skip, for paging.

items.description: pullRequestId, title, description, status, createdBy, sourceRefName, targetRefName, mergeStatus, isDraft and reviewers.

get_pull_request.title: Get a pull request
get_pull_request.description:
One pull request in full: its branches, status, reviewers with their votes, merge status and linked work items.
The two fields to read carefully are `mergeStatus` -- `conflicts` means it cannot be completed until someone rebases -- and `reviewers[].vote`, where 10 is approved, 5 approved with suggestions, 0 no vote, -5 waiting for the author and -10 rejected.

include_commits.description: Include the commits on the pull request.

include_work_item_refs.description: Include references to the linked work items.

isDraft.description: Whether it is still a draft.

reviewers.description: Each with displayName, vote (10 approved, -10 rejected) and isRequired.

create_pull_request.title: Open a pull request
create_pull_request.description:
Create a pull request between two branches. Both `source_branch` and `target_branch` are FULL REFS -- `refs/heads/feature/login`, not `feature/login` -- and passing the short name is the usual cause of a confusing 400.
Set `is_draft` to open it without notifying reviewers or triggering required policies, which is the right default for work in progress.
`work_item_refs` links work items to the pull request so they close automatically when it completes, each `{"id": "101"}`.
create_pull_request.notes: Branch names must be full refs. Opening a non-draft PR notifies reviewers and starts policy builds.

source_branch.description: The branch to merge from, as a full ref.

target_branch.description: The branch to merge into, as a full ref.

description.description: The pull request description. Markdown is rendered here.

is_draft.description: Open as a draft, which skips reviewer notifications and required policy runs until it is published.

reviewers.description: Reviewers to add, each {"id": "<identity-guid>"}. Add "isRequired": true to make one blocking.

work_item_refs.description: Work items to link, each {"id": "101"}. Linked items close automatically when the pull request completes.

mergeStatus.description: queued while Azure DevOps works out whether it merges cleanly.

update_pull_request.title: Update, complete or abandon a pull request
update_pull_request.description:
Change a pull request's title, description, target branch or status.
`status` is the consequential argument: setting it to `completed` MERGES the pull request -- irreversibly, and only if `mergeStatus` is `succeeded` and every required policy has passed. Setting it to `abandoned` closes it without merging, which is reversible by setting it back to `active`.
`completion_options` controls how the merge happens: `{"deleteSourceBranch": true, "mergeStrategy": "squash", "bypassPolicy": false}`. Leave bypassPolicy alone unless you mean to override the branch policies someone set deliberately.
update_pull_request.notes: status "completed" performs the merge and cannot be undone. Setting completion_options.bypassPolicy overrides branch policies.

status.description: completed merges the pull request and cannot be undone. abandoned closes it without merging. active reopens an abandoned one.

target_branch.description: Retarget the pull request at a different branch, as a full ref.

is_draft.description: False publishes a draft, which notifies reviewers and starts policy runs.

completion_options.description: How to merge when completing, e.g. {"deleteSourceBranch": true, "mergeStrategy": "squash", "bypassPolicy": false}.

last_merge_source_commit.description: The source commit id the completion is based on, from get_pull_request. Required when completing, and guards against merging a stale head.

output.description: The pull request after the change.

create_pull_request_thread.title: Comment on a pull request
create_pull_request_thread.description:
Start a comment thread on a pull request. Without `thread_context` the comment lands on the overview; with it, the comment attaches to a specific line of a specific file:
`{"filePath": "/src/app.ts", "rightFileStart": {"line": 42, "offset": 1}, "rightFileEnd": {"line": 42, "offset": 20}}`
`right` is the version after the change and `left` before it, so a comment on a deleted line uses `leftFileStart` instead.
Set `status` to `active` for a comment that must be resolved before the pull request completes when policy requires it.

pull_request_id.description: The pull request to comment on.

content.description: The comment text. Markdown is rendered.
content.example: This needs a null check before the dereference.

status.description: active for a comment that needs resolving, closed for one that does not, fixed to mark it already addressed.

thread_context.description: Where to anchor the comment in the diff -- filePath plus rightFileStart and rightFileEnd (or leftFile* for removed lines). Omit for a comment on the overview.

list_builds.title: List pipeline runs
list_builds.description:
Builds (pipeline runs) in a project, newest first, with their status, result, source branch and timings. `status_filter` of `inProgress` shows what is running now; `result_filter` of `failed` shows what broke.
`definitions` narrows to specific pipelines by id, which is what you want once a project has many.

definitions.description: Comma-separated pipeline definition ids to filter by.

branch_name.description: Only runs from this branch, as a full ref.

result_filter.description: Only completed runs with this result.

min_time.description: Only runs finished after this ISO 8601 time.

max_time.description: Only runs finished before this ISO 8601 time.

items.description: id, buildNumber, status, result, sourceBranch, sourceVersion, definition, requestedFor, startTime and finishTime.

get_build.title: Get a pipeline run
get_build.description: One build in full -- its status, result, the commit it ran against, who queued it and how long it took. `result` is only meaningful once `status` is `completed`; a run still in progress has no result yet, which is a common source of confused polling.

result.description: succeeded, partiallySucceeded, failed or canceled. Only set once completed.

list_build_definitions.title: List a project's pipelines
list_build_definitions.description:
The build pipeline definitions in a project, each with its id, name, path and queue status. The ids here are what queue_build and list_builds' `definitions` filter take.
A definition whose `queueStatus` is `paused` or `disabled` will silently not run when triggered, which is worth checking before debugging a trigger.

items.description: id, name, path, type, queueStatus, revision and createdDate.

queue_build.title: Run a pipeline
queue_build.description:
Queue a pipeline run. This EXECUTES whatever the pipeline does -- which may deploy to production, publish a package or change infrastructure. Read the definition before triggering one you did not write.
`source_branch` is a full ref and decides which version of the YAML runs as well as which code is built. `parameters` is a JSON STRING, not an object -- `"{\"environment\":\"staging\"}"` -- which is one of this API's less helpful corners.
Returns immediately with the build id; poll get_build until `status` is `completed`.
queue_build.notes: Runs the pipeline for real, which may deploy or publish. parameters is a JSON-encoded string, not an object.

definition_id.description: The pipeline definition id, from list_build_definitions.

source_branch.description: The branch to run against, as a full ref. Also decides which version of the pipeline YAML is used.

source_version.description: A specific commit id to build. Defaults to the branch head.

parameters.description: Pipeline variables as a JSON-ENCODED STRING, e.g. "{\"environment\":\"staging\"}". Not a JSON object.

reason.description: Why the build was queued, recorded on the run.

id.description: The build id; poll get_build with it.

cancel_build.title: Cancel a running pipeline run
cancel_build.description: Stop a build that is in progress. Anything the pipeline has already done -- files published, resources deployed -- stays done: cancelling stops further steps, it does not roll back. A pipeline cancelled part way through a deployment can leave the target in a half-changed state.
cancel_build.notes: Does not roll back. Steps already completed stay completed.

status.description: cancelling, then completed with result canceled.

get_build_timeline.title: Get a build's step-by-step timeline
get_build_timeline.description:
Every stage, job, task and step of a build, each with its own state, result, timings and error issues. This is where a failure's real cause lives: `get_build` says the run failed, and the timeline says which task failed and what it printed.
Look at `records[].issues` for the error messages, and at `records[].log.url` for the full log of a step.

output.description: The build's timeline of stages, jobs and tasks.

records.description: Each with id, parentId, type, name, state, result, startTime, finishTime, issues and log.
